newsitem.title: USA: Judge grants Singapore trip in spy case.
newsitem.headline: Judge grants Singapore trip in spy case.

text.p: A federal judge agreed on Friday to send a court-appointed lawyer to Singapore to help prepare the defence of accused CIA double-agent Harold Nicholson.
But District Judge James Cacheris denied permission for Nicholson, the highest-ranking Central Intelligence Agency officer charged with espionage, to make the trip in the custody of U.S. marshals.

At a pre-trial hearing on defence motions in Alexandria, Virginia, Cacheris cited an earlier ruling denying Nicholson bond as a flight risk. He also cited the government's argument that espionage was not an extraditable offence in Singapore.
The government has alleged that Nicholson handed classified documents to Russian agents in Singapore on June 27, 1996, after travelling there privately.

Court papers in the case filed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation detailed how Nicholson allegedly sought to shake anyone tailing him in Singapore before tucking a camera bag in the trunk of a car bearing dipomatic plates registered to the Russian embassy.

Liam O'Grady, one of Nicholson's two co-lead attorneys, told the judge that the defence would also ask the court to pay for defence trips to Kuala Lumpur, Moscow and Paris. He later said he had no idea when the defence might travel to Singapore or elsewhere.

Nicholson, 46, has pleaded not guilty to selling national security secrets to Moscow for 29 months until his Nov. 16 arrest. Prosecutors may seek the death penalty if he is convicted in a jury trial scheduled to begin April 14.

Nicholson was a 16-year CIA veteran who served as station chief in Romania from 1990 to 1992 before becoming deputy chief of station and operations officer in Malaysia. Earlier, he was posted to the Philippines, Thailand and Japan.
Cacheris rejected another defence motion seeking suppression of evidence gathered through warrantless searches authorised by a secret national security court.

Nicholson is seeking the first full-scale Supreme Court review of the recently expanded 1978 Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA). President Bill Clinton signed Executive Order 12949 on Feb. 9, 1995, giving the FISA court power to authorise physical searches in addition to wiretaps and other electronic surveillance.
In his ruling, Cacheris said case law on the Constitution's Fourth Amendment ban on unreasonable searches put physical entry and electronic surveillance on "an even plane."
"Accordingly, the physical searches in question here are constitutionally indistinguishable from the FISA-authorised electronic surveillance unanimously upheld by federal courts," he said.

The judge declined a request to cite his authority as a way of reassuring potential defence witnesses among Nicholson's former CIA colleagues. The government has agreed to let the defence send all CIA employees an e-mail message seeking their help in the case.

Jonathan Shapiro, Nicholson's other co-lead counsel, had sought to invoke the court's authority in the e-mail to "give a message to employees of the CIA that truly nothing will happen to them" if they step forward.

In opposing that request, Assistant U.S. Attorney Tom Connolly, one of the prosecutors, assured the court that he and his colleagues would make sure that "nothing adverse" happens to any defence witness from CIA ranks.
